usage: 썰다 is the verb for slicing long things; takes 를
produce sold tied in a bundle is counted with 단, never 개
넣다 = put into a pot; the all-purpose 'add an ingredient' verb
들어가다 describes an ingredient that belongs in the recipe
examples: 국에 대파 좀 넣어 주세요.
Please add some green onion to the soup.
casual cooking request; 좀 softens it to 'a bit'
마트에서 대파 한 단 샀어요.
I bought a bunch of green onion at the mart.
everyday shopping; counter 단 in action
대파를 송송 썰어서 국 위에 올렸어요.
I chopped the green onion into little rounds and put it on top of the soup.
real cooking; 송송 썰다 = chop into tiny crosswise rounds
nuance: 대파 is the thick, long, white-and-green scallion that anchors almost every Korean soup, stew, and stir-fry — the 대 means 'large', distinguishing it from the slim 쪽파 (small bunching onion) and the round-bulb 양파 (onion). English speakers reach for 'green onion' and assume one word covers all of them, but at a Korean market 대파, 쪽파, 양파, and 마늘쫑 are four different products in four different spots. The single biggest pitfall is the counter: 대파 is bundled and sold by the 단 (bunch), so '대파 한 단' is natural while '대파 한 개' sounds like you are pointing at one lonely stalk. It pairs habitually with 썰다/넣다 and especially the mimetic 송송 썰다 for chopping it into little rings dropped on top of a dish.

mistakes: Saying 대파 한 개 — produce tied in a bundle takes 단, so it should be 대파 한 단; 개 makes it sound like a single odd stalk.
Using 대파 when you mean the round onion 양파 — they are different vegetables, and a 직역 of English 'onion' will not tell them apart.
Mixing up 대파 with the thin 쪽파; 쪽파 is for 파전/garnish, while 대파 is the workhorse for soups and stir-fries.

usage: 넣다 for stirring it into a dish; takes 를
매워요 is from 맵다 (ㅂ-irregular), describing heat
powders are measured by the 스푼 (spoonful), not 개
뿌리다 = scatter on top, as a finishing dusting
examples: 김치찌개에 고춧가루를 더 넣었어요.
I added more chili powder to the kimchi stew.
simple; 더 = 'more', the everyday way to adjust heat
고춧가루가 없어서 색깔이 안 빨개요.
Because there's no chili powder, the color isn't red.
everyday cause-and-effect; -아서 links reason to result
고춧가루를 너무 많이 넣으면 안 매운 사람은 못 먹어요.
If you add too much chili powder, people who can't handle spice won't be able to eat it.
real situation; 못 먹다 = physically can't eat it
nuance: 고춧가루 is the dried, ground red-chili powder that gives Korean food its signature red color and heat — literally 고추(chili) + 가루(powder). Do not confuse it with 고추장, the fermented red-chili paste: 가루 is dry and dusty, 장 is a thick sticky paste, and they are not interchangeable in a recipe. The notorious spelling trap is the 사이시옷: because the compound 고추 + 가루 forms a tense [까] sound, Korean inserts ㅅ, giving 고춧가루, NOT 고추가루 — a mistake even some natives make in casual texting. Compared with Western cayenne it is coarser and milder by volume, so Korean recipes pour it in by the 스푼. It collocates with 넣다 (stir in) and 뿌리다 (sprinkle on top), and its heat is described with 맵다.

mistakes: Writing 고추가루 without the ㅅ — the 사이시옷 is required, so the correct spelling is 고춧가루.
Confusing 고춧가루 (dry powder) with 고추장 (thick fermented paste); they behave completely differently in cooking.
Pluralizing or counting it like a countable thing (고춧가루 한 개) — it is a powder, measured with 스푼/그램, e.g. 고춧가루 한 스푼.

usage: I drizzle cooking oil around the pan
두르다 = coat a pan by swirling oil around it
떨어지다 = run out / be used up (stock is gone)
에 marks the medium you fry IN
bottled liquids are counted with 병
examples: 팬에 식용유를 두르세요.
Coat the pan with cooking oil.
simple instruction; 두르다, not 넣다, for greasing a pan
식용유가 다 떨어져서 사러 가야 해요.
The cooking oil ran out, so I have to go buy some.
everyday errand; -아서 reason + 야 하다 obligation
튀김은 식용유를 많이 써서 기름값이 꽤 들어요.
Deep-frying uses a lot of oil, so the oil cost adds up quite a bit.
real situation; 들다 = (money) is required/spent
nuance: 식용유 is the everyday neutral frying oil (usually soybean or canola) — a Sino-Korean compound 食用油 meaning 'food-use oil', i.e. oil fit for eating, as opposed to industrial oil. The crucial contrast is with the aromatic finishing oils 참기름 (sesame) and 들기름 (perilla): 식용유 is the bland workhorse you cook IN, while 참기름/들기름 are fragrant seasonings you add at the END for flavor — never deep-fry in them. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb. In English you 'put oil in the pan', but Korean uses 두르다 (swirl/coat around) for greasing a pan: '식용유를 두르다' is natural, whereas '식용유를 넣다' sounds like you are pouring it into a soup. It collocates with 두르다 (coat), 튀기다 (deep-fry), and is counted by the 병.

mistakes: Using 식용유 when you mean a flavoring oil like 참기름 — 식용유 is for cooking IN, not for the nutty finishing aroma.
Saying 식용유를 넣다 to mean greasing a pan — the idiomatic verb is 두르다 (swirl it around), so 식용유를 두르다.
Assuming it is one specific oil; 식용유 is a generic category (soybean, canola, etc.), the way English 'cooking oil' covers several oils.

usage: 넣다 for adding a small amount; takes 을 after a consonant
냄새가 나다 = a smell comes off / is given off
I dress it with perilla oil
무치다 = toss/dress a vegetable side dish by hand
tiny liquid amounts are counted with 방울 (drop)
examples: 나물에 들기름을 조금 넣었어요.
I added a little perilla oil to the seasoned greens.
simple; 조금 = a little, matching its small-amount use
들기름은 금방 상하니까 냉장고에 넣어 두세요.
Perilla oil goes bad quickly, so keep it in the fridge.
everyday advice; -아 두다 = do and leave it that way
할머니가 직접 짠 들기름이라 향이 정말 진해요.
It's perilla oil my grandmother pressed herself, so the aroma is really deep.
real situation; 짜다 = press/extract oil, (이)라 = since it is
nuance: 들기름 is perilla-seed oil — 들(perilla/wild) + 기름(oil) — with a bold, nutty, earthy aroma that defines many 나물 (seasoned greens) and is brushed on 김 (laver). Its constant counterpart is 참기름, sesame oil (참 = 'true/genuine'): both are fragrant finishing oils, but 참기름 is lighter, sweeter, more universal, while 들기름 is heavier, grassier, and more regional/seasonal — a Korean cook chooses between them deliberately. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, treating it like generic 'oil' (식용유) and trying to fry in it — you don't; you add a 방울 at the finish. Second, storing it at room temperature: 들기름 oxidizes and turns rancid fast, so '냉장 보관' is the rule. It collocates with 무치다 (dress greens), 바르다 (brush on), and 향이 진하다 (deep aroma).

mistakes: Confusing 들기름 (perilla, grassy/heavy) with 참기름 (sesame, lighter/sweeter) — Koreans pick one on purpose for each dish.
Storing 들기름 at room temperature; it goes rancid quickly, so it should be refrigerated (냉장 보관).
Using 들기름 as a frying oil like 식용유 — it is a finishing aroma added in drops (한 방울), not a deep-frying medium.

usage: 뿌리다 = scatter on top as a finishing garnish
넣다 for mixing it into a dish; 을 after consonant
조금 = a small amount, the typical quantity
고소하다 = the toasty-nutty flavor of sesame/oil
examples: 마지막에 깨소금을 뿌리세요.
Sprinkle sesame salt at the end.
simple step; 마지막에 = at the very end, when it's added
나물에 깨소금을 솔솔 뿌리니까 더 고소해요.
Sprinkling sesame salt over the greens makes it nuttier.
everyday; 솔솔 = lightly/evenly scattering
깨소금만 넣어도 밥반찬이 훨씬 맛있어져요.
Just adding sesame salt alone makes a rice side dish taste much better.
real situation; -만 …-아도 = even just X is enough
nuance: 깨소금 is toasted sesame seeds ground with a little salt — 깨(sesame) + 소금(salt) — used as a finishing seasoning scattered over 나물, 무침, and other 반찬. The flavor it gives is described by the very Korean word 고소하다 (toasty, nutty, oily-rich), a taste that has no neat English match; it is NOT 'savory' (감칠맛) and not 'salty' (짜다). Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, the name says 소금(salt), so learners assume it is mostly salt, but it is mostly sesame — its job is aroma, not saltiness. Second, timing: 깨소금 is a finishing touch added at the very end (마지막에), because grinding and heat dull the toasty smell. Note that in casual kitchen talk many Koreans also loosely call plain toasted whole sesame seeds 깨소금. It collocates with 뿌리다 and the mimetic 솔솔.

mistakes: Assuming 깨소금 is basically salt because of the 소금 in the name — it is mostly toasted sesame; the point is aroma, not saltiness.
Adding it early in cooking; 깨소금 is a finishing garnish (마지막에 뿌리다), since heat kills the toasty 고소함.
Translating its taste as 'savory'; the right word is 고소하다 (nutty/toasty), which is distinct from 감칠맛 (umami-savory).

usage: 넣다 for adding it to a dish; 을 after consonant
알싸하다 = the sharp tingling kick of ginger (not 맵다)
다지다 = finely mince, the usual prep for ginger
생강차 = ginger tea; hot drinks counted with 잔
examples: 생강을 조금만 넣으세요.
Add just a little ginger.
simple; -만 = only/just, fitting its strong flavor
생강을 넣으면 고기의 비린내가 없어져요.
Adding ginger gets rid of the meat's gamey smell.
everyday tip; 비린내 = fishy/gamey off-smell
감기 기운이 있어서 생강차를 끓여 마셨어요.
I felt a cold coming on, so I brewed and drank ginger tea.
real situation; 감기 기운 = the early hint of a cold
nuance: 생강 is fresh ginger root, prized in Korean kitchens for killing the 비린내 (fishy/gamey smell) of meat and fish and for brewing 생강차 against colds. Its kick is best described by 알싸하다 (a sharp, tingling pungency) rather than 맵다 — 맵다 is the chili-heat of 고추, while ginger's bite is a different, almost numbing sharpness, so saying 생강이 매워요 sounds slightly off to natives. Watch the look-alike trap in recipes: 생강(ginger) sits right next to 마늘(garlic) in nearly every Korean marinade (the famous duo 생강·마늘), and beginners reading fast swap them. Because the flavor is so strong, recipes almost always pair it with 조금/조금만 (just a little) and the verb 다지다 (mince). It is usually peeled and minced, not sliced thick.

Swapping 생강 (ginger) and 마늘 (garlic) when reading a marinade — they appear together (생강·마늘) but are different roots.
Adding too much because the flavor seems mild raw; recipes call for 조금만, as 생강 quickly overpowers a dish.

usage: 우리다 = steep/draw flavor out into water
넣다 for dropping it into the pot; takes 를
flat sheet-like things are counted with 장
건지다 = fish/scoop solids out of liquid
examples: 물에 다시마를 한 장 넣으세요.
Put one sheet of kelp in the water.
simple; counter 장 for a flat piece of kelp
다시마는 물이 끓기 전에 건져 주세요.
Take the kelp out before the water boils.
everyday tip; -기 전에 = before (an action)
멸치하고 다시마를 같이 넣고 우리면 국물이 시원해요.
If you steep anchovies and kelp together, the broth comes out clean and refreshing.
real situation; 시원하다 = clean, bracing (of broth)
nuance: 다시마 is dried kelp, the backbone of Korean soup stock, almost always steeped together with 멸치 (dried anchovies) to build 육수. Do not confuse it with 미역, the other common seaweed: 다시마 is thick, leathery, and used to MAKE broth (then removed), whereas 미역 is thin, slippery, and EATEN in 미역국 (birthday/postpartum seaweed soup). The make-or-break tip — and the spot beginners ruin broth — is timing: pull the 다시마 out right before the water boils (끓기 전에 건지다); boil it too long and the broth turns slimy, cloudy, and bitter. It is counted by the flat 장 (sheet), and collocates with 우리다 (steep), 건지다 (scoop out), and 국물/육수 (broth). The 'good broth' compliment that results is 시원하다.

Letting 다시마 boil; you should 건지다 it right before boiling (끓기 전에), or the broth becomes slimy and bitter.
Counting it with 개; flat sheets of kelp take 장, so 다시마 한 장.

usage: (육수를) 내다 = produce stock by simmering — the set verb
진하다 = deep, strong, concentrated in flavor
우리다 = extract flavor into the water over time
examples: 멸치로 육수를 냈어요.
I made broth from anchovies.
simple; 로 = the means/material you make it from
이 집은 육수가 진하고 깊어서 인기가 많아요.
This place is popular because its broth is rich and deep.
everyday praise; 깊다 = deep, layered (of flavor)
육수가 부족하면 물을 조금 더 부으세요.
If the broth runs short, pour in a little more water.
real situation; 붓다 (ㅅ-irregular) = pour liquid
nuance: 육수 is the savory simmered stock at the base of soups, stews, and noodle dishes — Sino-Korean 肉水, literally 'meat-water', though in practice it is just as often drawn from 멸치 and 다시마, not only bones. The key contrast for learners is 육수 vs 국물: 육수 is the prepared stock you make on purpose as a base, while 국물 is simply 'the liquid in a dish' as served (the 국물 of your ramen, the 국물 of the kimchi). So you 육수를 내다 in advance, then ladle 국물 at the table. Two pitfalls: the 肉 character tempts English speakers to assume 육수 is always meat stock — it isn't. And the idiomatic verb is 내다/우리다 ('produce/steep' broth), not 만들다, so '육수를 내다' is what a cook says. Koreans judge a soup mainly by its 육수, praising it as 진하다 (rich) or 시원하다 (clean).

usage: 부치다 = pan-fry in a film of oil (same verb as for 전)
a pressed block of tofu is counted with 모
examples: 두부 한 모 주세요.
One block of tofu, please.
simple shop request; counter 모 in everyday use
두부를 노릇하게 부쳐서 간장에 찍어 먹어요.
I pan-fry tofu golden and eat it dipped in soy sauce.
everyday dish; 찍어 먹다 = dip-and-eat
순두부는 보통 두부보다 훨씬 부드러워서 숟가락으로 떠먹어요.
Soft tofu is much softer than regular tofu, so you scoop it up with a spoon.
real situation; 떠먹다 = scoop and eat
nuance: 두부 is tofu, sold in firm pressed blocks counted with the special unit 모 ('두부 한 모', never 한 개). The contrast to internalize is 두부 vs 순두부: regular 두부 is firm enough to slice and pan-fry, while 순두부 ('pure/silken tofu') is barely-set custard eaten with a spoon in 순두부찌개 — calling silken tofu plain 두부 will confuse a Korean cook. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: in English you 'fry' tofu, but Korean distinguishes 부치다 (pan-fry in a thin film of oil, the same verb used for 전/jeon) from 튀기다 (deep-fry in lots of oil); slices of tofu are 부치다, not 튀기다. It collocates with 부치다 (pan-fry), 으깨다 (mash), 부드럽다 (soft), and the stews 된장찌개/순두부찌개. Texture words 부드럽다 and 단단하다 (firm) describe its grades.

mistakes: Counting 두부 with 개 — a block of tofu takes the counter 모, so 두부 한 모.
Calling silken tofu 두부; the spoonable kind is 순두부, and mixing them up changes the dish entirely.
Using 튀기다 (deep-fry) for slices of tofu — pan-frying them in a little oil is 부치다, the jeon verb.

usage: 무치다 = dress/toss greens by hand into a 무침 side dish
삶다 = boil in water until done; takes 을
examples: 콩나물을 살짝 삶으세요.
Boil the bean sprouts briefly.
simple; 살짝 = lightly/just a bit, key for keeping crunch
어제 과음해서 콩나물국으로 해장했어요.
I drank too much yesterday, so I had bean-sprout soup to cure the hangover.
everyday; 해장하다 = eat/drink to recover from drinking
콩나물은 너무 오래 삶으면 물러지고 비린내가 나요.
If you boil bean sprouts too long, they go mushy and smell beany-off.
real situation; 물러지다 = turn mushy, 비린내 = off-smell
nuance: 콩나물 are soybean sprouts — 콩(soybean) + 나물(edible greens) — the long ones with a yellow bean head, a dirt-cheap staple behind the side dish 콩나물무침 and the hangover soup 콩나물국. The must-know contrast is 콩나물 vs 숙주(나물): 콩나물 grow from soybeans (bigger head, firmer, faintly nutty), while 숙주 grow from mung beans (smaller, more delicate, used in 쌀국수/만두소) — Korean recipes specify one, and they are not swappable. Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, lumping both under 'bean sprouts' and grabbing the wrong one. Second, cooking time — the whole point is the 아삭한 (crunchy) texture, so you 살짝 삶다 (boil briefly); overboil and they go mushy (물러지다) and develop a beany 비린내. It collocates with 삶다, 무치다, 아삭하다, and counts by the 봉지.

usage: 노릇노릇하게 = the -하게 adverb form before a verb
it cooked to a golden brown
examples: 전을 노릇노릇 부치세요.
Pan-fry the jeon until golden-brown.
simple instruction; bare 노릇노릇 before the verb
생선이 노릇노릇하게 잘 구워졌어요.
The fish grilled up nicely to a golden brown.
everyday result; 구워지다 = get grilled (passive)
식빵을 노릇노릇하게 구우니까 겉은 바삭하고 속은 촉촉해요.
Toasting the bread golden-brown makes it crispy outside and moist inside.
real situation; 바삭하다 crispy, 촉촉하다 moist
nuance: 노릇노릇 is a 의태어 (mimetic word) for the appetizing golden-brown surface of food fried, grilled, or toasted just right — built by reduplicating 노릇 from the color root 노랗다 (yellow). Unlike a neutral color word, it carries a built-in 'cooked to perfection, looks delicious' judgment, so it is almost always positive; its opposite outcome is 타다 (to burn), and you would never call burnt food 노릇노릇. It attaches to cooking verbs in two shapes — bare 노릇노릇 or the adverb 노릇노릇하게 — typically with 굽다, 부치다, 튀기다, 익다, and pairs naturally with texture mimetics like 바삭바삭 (crispy). The English-speaker pitfalls: spell it 노릇노릇 (not 노룻노룻), and don't stretch it to mean simply 'yellow' — 노릇노릇 is specifically the cooked golden of a surface, not the color of a lemon or a shirt.
